segments.he: בנו הרבר' וואלף מבאסקיויץ הי' עושה משא ומתן והי' איש אמיד והי' רוצה להחזיק את אביו ר' שמואל הנ"ל אבל הוא לא רצה כי לא הי' נהנה משל אחרים והי' הולך בלבושים פשוטים כי לא הי' ידו משגת ללבושים נכבדים ובתו הי' לו יסורים מזה והי' מוכיח אותו על זה ושהוא יעשה לו מלבושים כראוי והשיבלו כנ"ל שאינו נהנה כל ימיו וכו' ולא הועיל כלום עד שנפל על עצה כי הוא מבזה ומבייש אותו בזה. כי העולם אינם יודעין שזה מחמת שאינו רוצה להניח ממנו ורק יאמרו מפני שהוא קמצן ע"כ לא נותן לאבין שילביש א"ע. ובזה לקח אותן שקיבל המלבושים מבנו. ואחר פטירתו מצאו כל החשבון שבנו הוציא עליו ושיחזרו לו כדי שלא יהנה משל אחרים:
segments.en:
The aforementioned Reb Volf of Baskivitz was once traveling for business. He came to a certain town and entered an inn whose owners were murderers — every man who lodged there they would murder and take his money. He did not know this, entered with his wagon, put it in the courtyard, unharnessed the horses, gave them fodder, was given food to eat and a separate room to sleep — and nothing suspicious occurred to him. Already it was night; he had studied and lay down to sleep.

He dreamed that his father Reb Shmuel came to him from the Upper World [for at that point Reb Shmuel had already passed away] and said: "What is wrong with you?! You are in great danger!" He woke up and said: "Dream-words neither help nor hinder" — and went back to sleep. His father came again and said: "Why are you sleeping? You are in great danger!" He paid no attention even to this, and slept on. His father came a third time and would not let him sleep — saying: "Vos shlofstu? Zey roteve dikh!" [Why are you sleeping? Go, save yourself!]

He woke himself and said: "This must mean something." He tried to leave the room and found it locked — the key was nowhere. He devised ways out until he climbed up and got out through the window into the courtyard. The courtyard was shut and locked. He saw his wagon standing without the horses harnessed. He thought carefully, got inside the wagon, and lay down on the floor in the darkness where he would not be seen.

After a short while he heard the courtyard gate being opened. The innkeeper's own son entered — he had been at the market until midnight and was tired, not wanting to go home, so he came into this inn. He opened the courtyard, immediately locked it again, and went to Reb Volf's room. He saw a candle burning and the bed made — and he lay down to sleep in Reb Volf's bed.

In the middle of the night the innkeeper himself entered straight to that room — extinguished the candle — went straight to the bed, thinking Reb Volf was sleeping there — and with the axe in his hand struck the sleeping person without looking at all at who it was. [This was his practice: in the middle of the night he would enter with an axe, extinguish the candle, strike the sleeping person, then lift the blanket off the body; in the morning he would bury him there and take his money.] He struck — and killed his own son. Then he departed.

Reb Volf had heard everything — his knees knocked together — and he gave praise and prayer to Hashem for saving him from certain death through his righteous father's merit. He remained on the wagon the entire night until morning.
